one_liner: 2013 proof-of-concept thread-caching allocator with a dedicated free-recycling thread; README claims about 2x faster than glibc and jemalloc.
what_it_does: An experimental multi-threaded allocator, written in 15 commits over two weeks in April-May 2013. The code that produced the README numbers is malloc2.cpp at commit 39e4d67, which exposes malloc2(int)/free2(char*) and is built together with its own benchmark main. It is not a malloc/free replacement: there is no realloc, calloc, aligned allocation, size lookup or interposition. fc_malloc.cpp and fc_malloc.h at HEAD are unfinished stubs that do not compile (undefined `len`, a `free` with no return type), and HEAD's bench.cpp drives a later fixed_pool.hpp design instead.
how_it_is_fast: It borrows the LMAX Disruptor single-writer idea. Each thread bump-allocates from its own 8 MB mmap page and pushes freed pointers into a private, non-atomic ring buffer (16K slots). One garbage-collector thread busy-polls every thread's ring and moves the pointers into a shared 1M-slot recycle ring. Allocating threads then claim 16 recycled blocks at a time with a single relaxed fetch_add, so the fast path is a thread-local cache pop with no locks or CAS.
when_to_use: As reading material on Disruptor-style allocator design: single-producer free queues per thread plus a dedicated recycler thread.
To reproduce a 2013-era producer-consumer microbenchmark with fixed-size blocks, cross-thread frees and a spare core for the recycler.
As a starting point for a fixed-size-class pool inside your own code, after you rewrite the synchronization with proper atomics and backpressure.
when_not_to_use: Anything in production: no license (issue #1 closed without one), abandoned since 2013-05-07, and the last commit message says the fixed_pool design 'still has multi-threaded' bugs.

Mixed allocation sizes: in the benchmarked malloc2.cpp, get_bin() ignores the size and returns the same bin for every request, so a recycled small block can be handed out for a larger request (heap overflow).

Programs that free in bursts faster than the single recycler thread can drain them: the per-thread garbage ring and the shared recycle ring have no backpressure, so the writer can lap the reader and pointers get dropped (leak) or recycled twice (double handout).
Machines without a spare core: the recycler thread busy-spins (its usleep is commented out) even when idle.
Programs that need memory returned to the OS: pages are never unmapped.

integration.dependencies: none for malloc2.cpp (its own disruptor.hpp, mmap_alloc.hpp, fast_rand.cpp); HEAD CMakeLists links the benchmark against jemalloc
integration.platforms: Linux and macOS (POSIX mmap); x86 rdtsc in fast_rand.cpp; Windows not supported despite CMake defines
integration.thread_safety: Claimed lock-free and thread-safe, but cross-thread handoff uses plain or volatile int64 fields with no acquire/release ordering (data races under the C++ memory model), and the rings can overflow (see when_not_to_use)

gotchas: The README says 128-byte allocations, but the benchmark at the commit that added the tables (39e4d67, malloc2.cpp) allocates 60 bytes (rounded to 64 plus a 16-byte header) and never touches the memory; HEAD bench.cpp instead allocates 10000 bytes into 32K-slot arrays with memset, a configuration that matches neither table.
free2() publishes its ring position only after more than 10 frees, so up to 10 frees per thread stay invisible to the recycler.

mmap_alloc checks `if(!limit)` instead of MAP_FAILED, so a failed mmap returns (char*)-1; on Linux it opens /dev/zero for every page and never closes the fd. The HEAD fixed_pool maps at address hints that encode the size class ((ItemSize<<32) + pos*PageSize) and only asserts that the hint was honoured; on macOS it passes MAP_FIXED to that address, which can clobber existing mappings.
Open issues #3-#5 (2020) report double allocation after block merging and duplicate ring-buffer claims in malloc3.cpp; none were answered.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Effectively never for use: IsoAlloc, Spaces or micromalloc are licensed, maintained, size-class-correct malloc replacements with real benchmarks. Read fc_malloc only for the Disruptor-style recycler-thread idea, which none of the catalogued siblings use.
verified_claims_summary: First-party wall times from one random producer-consumer run on unstated hardware, compiler and jemalloc version: 2.6 s vs 5.8 s glibc and 4.5 s jemalloc on 1 thread, and 6.8 s vs 18.2 s and 13.6 s on 10 threads; a second table shows 4.8-12.9 s vs jemalloc's 9.7-27.9 s at 1-10 threads with about 14% more RAM. The benchmarked allocator (malloc2.cpp at 39e4d67) serves one fixed 60-byte size, uses a spinning extra thread, and its unbounded-overwrite rings can drop or double-issue blocks under exactly this cross-thread free load, so the numbers do not describe a general-purpose, correct malloc.
status_note: Abandoned since 2013-05-07 with no license (all rights reserved) and HEAD sources that do not compile as a library; reference only.
